title: The Briefing: Could Arsenal end the season empty-handed? Will the FA Cup help or hinder Leeds survival hopes?
content:
Welcome to The Briefing, where every Monday, The Athletic discusses three of the biggest issues raised by the weekend’s action.

With the Premier League campaign on hold before it enters its final weeks, the FA Cup took centre stage over the past two days: Manchester City thrashing Liverpool on Saturday lunchtime, Chelsea enjoying a bit of shooting practice against Port Vale of League One, Championship side Southampton stunning top-flight leaders Arsenal, and finally Leeds United beating West Ham United on penalties to secure their first FA Cup semi-final appearance for 39 years.

Here, we will discuss the potential impact on matters at both ends of the Premier League, as well as the legacy of Bernardo Silva, whose end-of-season departure from Manchester City after nine years of trophy-filled service was confirmed on Sunday.

Let’s be clear about this. For all the external talk of a quadruple over the past weeks and months, Arsenal’s ambitions for this season never revolved around winning the Carabao Cup or FA Cup. The primary aims were always the Premier League and Champions League.

Manager Mikel Arteta’s selection of backup goalkeeper Kepa Arrizabalaga to start the Carabao Cup final against Manchester City last month illustrated that, as did his line-up for Saturday’s FA Cup quarter-final away to Southampton.

But Arteta was clear before their Wembley meeting that beating City would help Arsenal in pursuit of those higher goals. “Winning always helps — and winning a trophy helps more, for sure,” he said. “It gives you confidence. It gives you the feeling that, when it comes to that moment, you can do it and you have enough resources to achieve what you want.”

On that basis, Arsenal’s task for the weeks ahead has intensified.

The threat of fixture congestion has eased a little — no FA Cup semi-final or final on the horizon after their shock 2-1 loss to second-tier Southampton on Saturday night — but the psychological boost Arteta hoped for has not materialised. And if winning breeds confidence, doesn’t it stand to reason that back-to-back defeats might fuel a sense of anxiety “when it comes to that moment”?

Arsenal remain clear favourites to win the first Premier League, nine points clear of second-placed City (albeit having played a game more and with a trip to City awaiting in two weeks), and are strong contenders to win the Champions League, where they now travel to Lisbon to take on Sporting CP in the first leg of a quarter-final on Tuesday. Arteta has described this as “the most beautiful period of the season” — and if he and his team fulfil either of their prime objectives (a first Premier League championship since 2004 or winning the Champions League for the first time in club history), then it will be blissful for Arsenal’s supporters.

But there hasn’t been much beauty about Arsenal’s progress lately. It has been a slog for weeks — months, even — and it threatens to get harder now that the pressure has been cranked up another couple of notches. Nor does it help that City, with the Carabao Cup secured and through to another FA Cup semi-final, where they play Southampton, seem to be enjoying themselves for the first time all season.

That title showdown in Manchester on April 19 looks huge. But so does every game for Arsenal now.

Nuno Espirito Santo made five changes to West Ham’s starting line-up for their FA Cup quarter-final at home to fellow relegation candidates Leeds yesterday. A place in the FA Cup semi-finals was desirable, but survival in the Premier League is critical. Leeds coach Daniel Farke made three changes to his starting XI, admitting that avoiding the drop was “the priority”.

But there was something about Farke’s and Leeds’ approach — certainly until a pulsating tie entered second-half stoppage time — that showed greater intent. “It makes no sense to wrap the players in cotton wool,” he told reporters in his press conference on Friday. “We have the chance to achieve something special and unique. We want to grab this chance with both hands.”

Ultimately, Leeds grabbed the chance. Yes, it came down to penalties, after West Ham came from two down to level by scoring twice in stoppage time, but there was a sense of fortune favouring the brave as Leeds reached the competition’s semi-finals for the first time since 1987.

The question — as with Arsenal — is whether this result will impact these teams as the focus turns back to the Premier League.

West Ham are still in the relegation zone. Leeds are four points above them in 15th. For all the media focus on Tottenham Hotspur’s travails, this is a dogfight.

Nuno suggested afterwards that, whereas the psychological afterglow of victory would have fuelled his players’ physical recovery, the “sadness” of defeat might be harder to shake off. But shake it off they must, with a critical game at home to surely doomed and last-placed Wolverhampton Wanderers to come on Friday.

The obvious counterpoint is that Leeds will now have at least one more game to contend with over the coming weeks — and an FA Cup semi-final against Chelsea will take up plenty of bandwidth at Elland Road over the next three weeks. Midfielder Anton Stach and defender Joe Rodon also suffered injuries on Sunday.

For all the excitement generated by reaching those Wembley semi-finals, Premier League survival remains the overriding objective. Nobody at Leeds wants their season to end on May 24 — when they will be back at West Ham, as it happens — with relegation.

But there is much to be said for the positive energy that continuing this FA Cup run would bring. Farke, who often appears a more optimistic sort than Nuno, will certainly believe so.

Last night brought confirmation that Bernardo Silva will depart when his contract expires at the end of the season.

Wherever he ends up going next, Bernardo’s place among City’s all-time greats is assured. He has made 450 appearances for the club, the ninth-highest total in their history and most by any player since the 1980s. He has won 14 major trophies in a City shirt (and six more in the Community Shield, UEFA Super Cup and the old annual version of the Club World Cup), and few would bet against him, as their current captain, leading them to a third FA Cup success — and if he gets his way, a seventh Premier League title — on the way out.

His departure will not generate as many headlines or as much emotion as Mohammed Salah’s from Liverpool at the same time and after the same number of seasons — or indeed manager Pep Guardiola’s from City, should that also happen this summer — but we are talking about another of the leading players in the modern Premier League era. As Jordan Campbell wrote, after City’s 4-0 quarter-final victory against visitors Liverpool on Saturday, Bernardo is still their glue, brains and heartbeat.

Bernardo’s contribution has never been as strikingly obvious as those of Yaya Toure, Kevin De Bruyne and Sergio Aguero at City, or some of the swashbuckling, show-stopping Premier League midfield legends of the past, but it has been huge nonetheless. His intelligence, his understanding of space, his abundant technical qualities, his non-stop running and his underrated competitive instincts have made him one of the outstanding midfielders in world football over the past decade.

You will often hear Guardiola suggest that, when players wish to leave to City, he does not stand in their way. But he certainly stood in Bernardo’s way when the Portugal international floated the idea on several occasions over the past nine years, particularly in the summers of 2021, 2022 and 2023. There are some players worth making exceptions for — and Guardiola must be glad he did.
